posts.quote: Back In 11 Days. Nvidia's Huang Quit In A Spy Scandal. Then Trump Said Rehire Him. The Board Caved
posts.alt: Photo of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a black leather jacket, looking off to the side, with a circle inset of President Donald Trump's official portrait. Headline text: Back In 11 Days. Nvidia's Huang Quit In A Spy Scandal. Then Trump Said Rehire Him. The Board Caved.
posts.caption:
Eleven days. That's how long Nvidia lasted without Jensen Huang.

Here's how it went down.

On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia. Reports had come out about extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company buying Nvidia chips. U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe she was working for Chinese intelligence. Huang had already admitted to staff that he cheated on his wife.

Finance chief Colette Kress was named interim CEO. The board named its first-ever chair, Harvey Jones. And on November 17, Kress shut the door on CNBC: "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen."

Case closed. Right?

Wrong. Late on November 22, President Trump posted on Truth Social: "I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A."

The next morning, Nvidia announced the board had voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president and CEO, effective immediately. The stock jumped 31% in one day.

Trump went on CNBC and didn't sugarcoat it. He said Huang "had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong." Then: "you have to protect our geniuses. We don't have enough of them."

Say what you want about his personal life. That part was ugly, and he admitted it. But America does not win the chip race by benching its best player while China watches. Trump said it out loud. The board agreed.
posts.first:
The facts: Nvidia's own press release says the board reinstated Huang as president, CEO and board member by unanimous vote, effective immediately. Its SEC filing dates the board action to November 22, and the announcement came November 23. Harvey Jones stays on as chair, and Kress stays CFO.

The board said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Huang's statement: "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution."

What is NOT settled: the spy claim comes from U.S. intelligence sources through the New York Times. Beijing denies it. Attorney General Todd Blanche said November 12 the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion. The board says its own investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort will "proceed to conclusion."

Sources: Nvidia press releases, SEC filing, AP, CNBC, Reuters, NPR.

posts.quote: A Backdoor Blasphemy Law? NJ Democrats Want Cops To Use A State Definition Of Islamophobia
posts.alt: Official portrait photo of New Jersey Assemblyman Joe Danielsen, prime sponsor of bill A1146, in a dark suit and green striped tie before U.S. and New Jersey flags, with a circle inset of the gold New Jersey State House dome. Headline text: A Backdoor Blasphemy Law? NJ Democrats Want Cops To Use A State Definition Of Islamophobia.
posts.caption:
Sorry, but in America no religion gets a government shield from criticism. Not mine. Not anybody's.

New Jersey Democrats have a bill, A1146, that would create an official state definition of Islamophobia. Police and public officials would have to "take into consideration" that definition when deciding whether an alleged discriminatory act was motivated by anti-Muslim bias.

The list includes "hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture" and "rhetorical" manifestations. Rhetorical. As in words.

Former Navy SEAL and attorney Bill Brown called it a "backdoor blasphemy law." His warning: "The mere threat of state scrutiny is a direct assault on public debate."

Protect people. Never protect ideas from being questioned. That's the First Amendment.
posts.first:
The facts: A1146 is sponsored by Democratic Assemblyman Joe Danielsen with three Democratic co-sponsors. It was introduced January 13, 2026 and sits in the Assembly State and Local Government Committee with no hearing and no vote. None of the sponsors answered Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

To be fair, the bill creates no new crime and says it shall not "diminish or infringe upon any right protected under the First Amendment." Harassing anyone over their faith is already wrong and already illegal.

Sources: NJ Legislature (bill A1146), Fox News, Algemeiner.

posts.quote: Days After Putin's Peace Pledge, Medvedev Says Russia Could Be Obligated To Use Nukes
posts.alt: Photo of Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, glaring to the side, with a circle inset of Vladimir Putin. Headline text: Days After Putin's Peace Pledge, Medvedev Says Russia Could Be Obligated To Use Nukes.
posts.caption:
Four days after Trump, Putin and Xi declared "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," Dmitry Medvedev wrote this:

"Should the abovementioned scenarios unfold, the head of state is not only entitled but also obligated to use nuclear weapons."

Obligated. Peace through strength isn't optional.
posts.first:
The facts: Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote it in the Moscow Journal of International Law. Quote via TASS English, November 23.

Sources: TASS, RIA Novosti, White House.
